bloques.html:
Read the story and answer questions 7 to 12.

The Last Hundred Meters

Nico could see the summit. It was right there, a white tooth against the sky, no more than a hundred meters above them. For six hours he had climbed toward it, and for six months he had dreamed of it.

His aunt Carla stopped and looked west. Clouds were pouring over the far ridge like milk boiling over the edge of a pot.

"We turn around," she said.

"But we're almost there!" Nico's voice cracked. "Ten more minutes!"

"Twenty up, and twenty back to this spot. In forty minutes we will not be able to see our own boots." She was already coiling the rope. "The volcano will be here next summer, Nico. I intend for us to be here, too."

He wanted to argue. He wanted to sit down in the snow and refuse to move. Instead he looked at the clouds again. They had already swallowed the ridge.

He turned his back on the summit. It was the hardest step of the whole climb.

Halfway down, the wind arrived, and the world shrank to the red of Carla's jacket three meters ahead. Nico followed it without a word. He was no longer thinking about the summit. He was thinking that some people would have kept going, and that he was glad his aunt was not one of them.

bloques.html:
Read Text A and Text B and answer questions 13 to 18.

Text A — A Continent for Science (encyclopedia entry)

No owner. Antarctica is the only continent with no native population and no government. Seven countries, including Chile, claim parts of it. However, the Antarctic Treaty, signed in 1959, put those claims on hold and reserved the continent for peace and science.

Rules. Under the treaty, military activity is forbidden and scientists are free to do research. A later agreement banned mining.

Visitors. Tourism is allowed, and it is growing. Most visitors arrive by ship during the southern summer. Tour companies follow guidelines: for example, only a limited number of people may be ashore at one place at the same time. Scientists nevertheless worry that visitors could carry seeds or diseases to a place that has been isolated for millions of years.

Text B — Come and See It (advertisement by a cruise company)

Antarctica is the most breathtaking place on Earth, and you deserve to see it before it changes forever. On our ships, you will stand among thousands of penguins and watch ice cliffs fall into the sea.

Worried about the environment? Relax. Our guests are nature lovers, and nature lovers never cause harm. In fact, every visitor returns home as an ambassador for Antarctica, ready to defend it. We follow all the visitor guidelines, and our guides are trained biologists.

Book today. Places for next summer are almost gone!

Read the poem and answer questions 19 to 21.

The Observatory

All day the dome is a closed eyelid,
asleep on the mountain, dreaming of night.
At dusk it opens without a sound
and drinks the oldest light.

Some stars it watches are already gone,
burned out before the first word was said.
Their light keeps travelling, patient and thin,
a letter still waiting to be read.

pautaHtml:
Guion de Listening (leer dos veces, en voz alta)

Lee a ritmo normal, como quien cuenta un misterio en un documental. Pausa de 30 segundos entre lecturas. No expliques palabras. Texto creado para este examen, sobre un hecho real (las piedras de Racetrack Playa, en el Valle de la Muerte, California).

The Mystery of the Sailing Stones

In a desert valley in California, there is a dry lake bed that is almost perfectly flat. Scattered across it are rocks, some as small as an apple and some heavier than a person. Behind many of them stretches a long track in the dried mud, as if the rock had been dragged. For decades, nobody could explain it, because nobody had ever seen a rock move.

People suggested strong winds, magnetism, and even pranksters. But there were no footprints beside the tracks, and some of the rocks seemed far too heavy for wind alone.

Then a small team of researchers decided to stop guessing and start watching. They placed their own rocks on the lake bed, each one fitted with a GPS tracker. They set up a weather station. Then they waited, prepared to wait for many years.

In the winter of 2013 to 2014, they got lucky. Rain had left a shallow pond. At night it froze into a sheet of ice as thin as a windowpane. In the morning sun, the ice cracked into large floating panels, and a gentle breeze pushed those panels against the rocks. The rocks slid slowly across the soft mud, much slower than a person walking.

So the answer was not one thing. It was water, ice, sun and wind, in exactly the right order, in one of the driest places on Earth. No wonder it took so long to see.

Guion de Speaking (5 minutos)

Solo en inglés. El niño puede mirar el cuento. No corrijas durante la conversación; anota y califica al final con la rúbrica. En el paso 4 tomas a propósito la postura contraria a la suya: se evalúa cómo responde, no si te convence.

  1. Warm-up (30 s, no se califica): "What was the most interesting thing you learned this year, in any subject?"
  2. Summary (1 min): "Summarize 'The Last Hundred Meters' in about five sentences. Tell me who the characters are, what the problem is and how it ends." Apoyo: "What does Carla see?" / "What does Nico do in the end?"
  3. Opinion with reasons (1-2 min): "Was Carla right to turn around so close to the summit? Give me two reasons, and use one detail from the story as evidence." Apoyo: "Which words in the story make you think that?"
  4. Objection (1 min): si dijo que Carla tuvo razón: "But if you always turn back when there is a risk, you will never achieve anything difficult. What do you say to that?" Si dijo que no: "Carla said that in forty minutes they would not be able to see their own boots. What could have happened if they had continued?" Deja que responda sin interrumpir.
  5. Closing (30 s): "Tell me about a time when you had to stop doing something you really wanted to finish. What did you learn?" Cierre: "Thank you. That is the end of the exam."

Rúbricas

Escritura (ítem 29) — 9 puntos. Valen las dos posturas; se califica el argumento.

Criterio Puntos
Claim, reasons and evidence (0-3) 3: postura clara al inicio y dos razones distintas, cada una desarrollada, con al menos un dato correcto del texto A. 2: postura clara y dos razones, pero sin dato del texto A o con una razón apenas enunciada. 1: postura clara con una sola razón. 0: sin postura reconocible
Counterclaim and rebuttal (0-2) 2: presenta un argumento de la otra postura y lo responde con un motivo. 1: menciona la otra postura pero no la responde, o la responde sólo negándola. 0: no hay otra postura
Organización y conectores (0-2) 2: 10 a 12 oraciones en el orden pedido, cierre que retoma la postura y al menos tres conectores bien usados. 1: se reconoce el orden, pero falta el cierre, hay menos de 8 oraciones o un solo conector. 0: sin orden
Registro, variedad de oraciones y corrección (0-2) 2: registro formal, al menos dos oraciones complejas, máximo 3 errores de ortografía o puntuación. 1: algunos coloquialismos o contracciones, o 4 a 6 errores. 0: registro coloquial o errores que dificultan la lectura

Respuesta modelo: Tourists should be allowed to visit Antarctica, but only in small numbers and under strict rules. First, the Antarctic Treaty reserves the continent for peace and science, and it does not forbid tourism. A total ban would therefore go further than the treaty itself. In addition, people protect what they know: a visitor who has seen a penguin colony is more likely to care about its future. Admittedly, scientists worry that visitors could carry seeds or diseases to a place that has been isolated for millions of years. This concern is serious. However, it can be reduced with rules that already exist, such as limiting the number of people who may be ashore at one place. Companies that break those rules should lose the right to travel there. For these reasons, the question is not whether tourists should visit Antarctica, but how many and how carefully. Visits should continue only while they leave no trace.

Qué mira este instrumento

Examen acumulativo del año al nivel Cambridge Primary English Stage 6 (inglés como primera lengua) y Common Core ELA Grade 5. Parte 1, comprensión auditiva de una charla de divulgación con inferencia e idea principal (1-6). Parte 2, cuento en tercera persona: punto de vista, lenguaje figurado, inferencia, tema y evidencia textual (7-12; contenidos de S1 y S3). Parte 3, dos textos sobre un tema: características del texto, resumen, propósito, hecho y opinión, y cruce de fuentes (13-18; S2 y S4). Parte 4, poema: metáfora y relación entre estrofas (19-21; S3). Parte 5, lenguaje: tiempos verbales (S1), comparativos y adverbios (S2), puntuación, voz pasiva, raíces (S4), diálogo y oración compleja (22-28). Parte 6, texto de opinión con contraargumento (29; S5). Parte 7, speaking (30). Todos los textos de lectura y el poema son textos creados para este examen; el aviso del texto B es de una empresa ficticia.

Control Mineduc: el examen cubre los cuatro ejes de Inglés 5º, comprensión auditiva (OA1-4), comprensión de lectura (OA5-9), expresión oral (OA10-13) y escritura (OA14-16). Todos se dan por superados para este niño: los OA apuntan a textos breves y simples con apoyo visual y funciones básicas (saludar, describir, expresar gustos), y aquí trabaja como hablante nativo de 5º-6º grado.

Datos factuales del material. Seguros: el Tratado Antártico se firmó en 1959, siete países (entre ellos Chile) reclaman territorio y el tratado dejó esos reclamos en suspenso, un acuerdo posterior prohibió la minería, y los operadores turísticos limitan cuántas personas desembarcan a la vez; la Antártica es el continente más frío y ventoso. El texto A dice que el continente no tiene gobierno y que los reclamos están "on hold": es la formulación del tratado, no una opinión sobre el Territorio Chileno Antártico. Dato en que convendría verificar antes de imprimir: en el guion de Listening, que la observación directa de las piedras en movimiento fue en el invierno de 2013 a 2014 y que el equipo usó rocas con GPS y una estación meteorológica (lo cito de memoria, de un estudio publicado en 2014).

Señales por parte: si falla 7-12 pero acierta 13-18, el punto débil es la lectura literaria (inferir y explicar el efecto), no la comprensión. Si falla 15-18, lee el contenido pero no al autor. Si falla 22-23, quedan vacíos de S1 y S2 (formas del pasado y comparativos), que son de forma escrita y no de idioma. Si falla 24, 25 y 27, falta gramática y puntuación explícitas, que en un niño bilingüe suelen ir por detrás del oído. Si en 29 pierde el criterio de contraargumento, repetir la semana 5.

Si le fue mal

  • Lectura literaria: repasar la guía 3 y hacer la misión "The narrator swap" con una escena de un libro que esté leyendo.
  • Dos textos: repasar la guía 4; buscar un aviso y un artículo sobre el mismo producto o lugar y comparar propósito y hechos.
  • Gramática y puntuación: una oración al día para corregir o transformar (activa a pasiva, dos oraciones a una compleja, diálogo sin puntuar).
  • Argumento: repasar la guía 5 y escribir un texto de opinión por semana con el plan de cinco partes; el adulto hace siempre una objeción.
  • Para las vacaciones: leer una novela en inglés de nivel 5º-6º grado y conversar cada capítulo con tres preguntas fijas: quién cuenta, qué cambió, qué frase lo prueba.
